children: plans to put a new generation of its internally designed artificial intelligence chips into data centers in the first half of next year, with the company targeting lower energy use and costs for running AI models.

The third-generation processor, MTIA 450, code-named Arke, is currently being tested, while its successor, MTIA 500, or Astrid, is expected to complete design work in about a month and enter data centers by the end of 2027, Yee Jiun Song, Meta's VP of engineering, said in an interview with Bloomberg.
“Each one takes on a little bit more risk technologically and gets us better performance,” Song said, referring to the progression of Meta's
custom chips. He said that includes better performance per watt and per dollar.
The Facebook parent is working with Broadcom
on chip designs and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company
on production. The company has committed to more than a gigawatt of the chips over a 12-month period, Song said, adding that it expects deployment to accelerate afterward if AI demand remains strong.
Twelve Arke chips arrived from TSMC
on September 1, with performance within 2% to 3% of simulations. The processors have already run Meta
models as well as models from DeepSeek (
canceled its planned Olympus chip, which was intended for both AI training and inference, partly because of cost concerns. The company is instead focusing on inference.
“These are the workhorse chips that we’re going to use for general-purpose inference,” Song said.
The company expects future chip generations to improve speed and throughput, with Song saying Meta
has “a very robust roadmap” for custom silicon.

title: Meta plans wider use of in-house AI chips as it targets lower costs
